s1.syndrome_frame: Acute episodic neurological syndrome with abdominal pain, vomiting, and altered mental status
salient_findings: Diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact
Frontal headache and persistent nausea after the episode
key_facts: 8-year-old boy with no significant past medical history
30-minute history of generalized abdominal pain
Single episode of vomiting
Developed diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact
Episode lasted 10 minutes
Reported a frontal headache (5/10) and persistent nausea after the episode
Family denied toxin or medication exposure
Similar episode 18 months earlier
No personal or family history of epilepsy or neurological disorders
Developmental milestones were age-appropriate
Normal vital signs except for blood pressure above the 95th percentile for age
Neurologic examination revealed confusion and disorientation
Normal motor and sensory examinations
Consciousness and orientation improved approximately 20 minutes after arrival
Had three additional self-limited vomiting episodes and ongoing headache
Headache improved after a single IV dose of diclofenac (1 mg/kg)
Complete blood count, serum chemistries, and electrolytes were all within normal limits
Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol was reported as normal for age

shortlist.label: Migraine with abdominal aura
shortlist.why_kept: Patient has a history of similar episode diagnosed as migraine and current episode has headache and abdominal pain

shortlist.label: Cyclic vomiting syndrome
shortlist.why_kept: Patient has recurrent episodes of vomiting and abdominal pain

shortlist.label: Abdominal epilepsy
shortlist.why_kept: Patient has episodes of altered mental status and abdominal pain

shortlist.label: Acute intermittent porphyria
shortlist.why_kept: Patient has episodes of abdominal pain, vomiting, and altered mental status, which are common symptoms of porphyria

shortlist.label: Pancreatitis
shortlist.why_kept: Patient has severe abdominal pain and vomiting, which are common symptoms of pancreatitis

raw.rationale: The patient's symptoms, including generalized abdominal pain, vomiting, diaphoresis, and headache, are consistent with migraine, and the episode's self-limited nature and improvement with diclofenac support this diagnosis. The patient's history of a similar episode 18 months earlier, diagnosed as migraine, further supports this diagnosis.

rejected.label: Cyclic vomiting syndrome
rejected.why: While the patient had multiple vomiting episodes, the presence of abdominal pain, diaphoresis, and headache suggests a more complex condition like migraine.

rejected.label: Abdominal epilepsy
rejected.why: The patient's normal EEG and brain MRI, as well as the lack of personal or family history of epilepsy, make this diagnosis less likely.

rejected.label: Acute intermittent porphyria
rejected.why: The patient's normal serum chemistries and electrolytes, as well as the lack of other symptoms like muscle weakness or neurological deficits, make this diagnosis unlikely.

rejected.label: Pancreatitis
rejected.why: The patient's normal serum chemistries and electrolytes, as well as the lack of other symptoms like severe abdominal tenderness or guarding, make this diagnosis unlikely.
